newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Kohl reform bid fails to shake up Germany.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Kohl reform bid fails to shake up Germany.

text.p: Halving unemployment, cutting taxes, reducing bloated labour costs and slashing state borrowing to qualify for the European single currency: the German government made a lot of promises in 1996.

But as the year draws to a close, most of those pledges are unravelling and the jury is still out on whether Finance Minister Theo Waigel can control spending in 1997 enough to lead monetary union from the front.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl racked up his 14th year in office, outlasting his mentor Konrad Adenauer, and at the middle of his fourth term should have been able to pass tough reforms needed to make Germany's high-cost economy more competitive.
But Kohl's long years in power belied the weakness of his fractious coalition, the opposition's new-found stubbornness, and deep public scepticism that things will really change.
LOOKING LIKE A PLUCKED CHICKEN
"The government looks like a heavily-plucked chicken -- it hasn't got many feathers left," Thomas Mayer, economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt, said of Kohl's policy setbacks.
One by one, government goals have fallen by the wayside. An "alliance for jobs" with trade unions to halve unemployment by the turn of the century collapsed.
Instead of falling, dole queues set post-war records from month to month, reaching four million in November. Forecasters say unemployment will rise next year and stay high.

Revenues fell short and soaring unemployment blew a hole in the state benefits system which Waigel had to fill from federal coffers. This year's budget deficit will be near four percent of gross domestic product -- above the Maastricht treaty's three percent target.

Waigel says borrowing will fall to 2.5 percent of GDP next year. But economists say that despite bold spending cuts, the goal optimistically assumes 2.5 percent growth. Recovery could be strangled by surging social costs, they warn.
SICK PAY CLIMBDOWN HITS WELFARE CUTS
The government had hoped to hand German employers a big cash windfall by passing a law allowing a one-fifth cut in sick pay benefits, which have been the most generous in Europe.
But the measure, part of a jobs and growth programme, drew a hostile response from trade unions who saw it as a first step towards dismantling Germany's featherbed welfare state.
Hundreds of thousands thronged the capital Bonn in the summer to oppose the cuts, and widespread protests by industry workers forced employers finally to cave in in December.

"Germany's social problems mean the smallest steps -- and in relative terms cutting sick pay was a tiny change -- cannot be pushed through," Klaus-Peter Schoeppner, head of the Emnid opinion research institute, told Reuters.
FISCAL TIME-BOMBS STILL TICKING
Slight progress in freeing up the jobs market and trimming welfare costs was reversed by a move to hike pension charges in 1997 to stop the pay-as-you-go system from going bust.
Health insurance charges may have to rise too and economists say the overstretched jobless insurance scheme could need billions of marks more in cash help next year.

The huge pressure on state finances came close to tearing apart Kohl's three-party coalition after the Free Democrat (FDP) junior coalition balked at tax hikes. The FDP eventually agreed to delay cutting the unpopular solidarity surcharge, which funds aid to east Germany, by a year to 1998.
TAX CONFLICT CERTAIN
The Social Democrats (SPD), shedding their image as a lame-duck opposition, wielded their majority in the upper house of parliament to delay Waigel's 1997 tax bill for weeks.

The SPD finally gave up its bid to keep wealth taxes in the face of what leader Oskar Lafontaine called the government's "ice-cold blackmail". But the SPD chief pledged to make wealth tax a votewinner in general elections due in 1998.
So, while the governing coalition finalises its plans for a major reform to cut income tax in 1999 and scrap a range of tax breaks, further conflict with the SPD is certain.

Newspaper criticism of the goings-on has been withering. "The results of the tax poker in Bonn and the wage poker in the country are becoming ever more alike. You don't give in to me, so I won't give in to you. In the end everone is satisfied, but nothing happens," financial daily Handelsblatt said.
But pollsters say that, if Kohl's team can draft sound tax reforms and convince voters monetary union will go ahead for sure, that could shake Germany out of its stagnant mood.

"Germans are still happy, but they realise things can't go on like this," Schoeppner said. "The longer the tax debate goes on, the higher the expectations will be that the reform will provide the spark for real change in Germany."
But Germans, who still cling to the social market model that drove the country's post-war economic miracle, will not have had their confidence in reforms helped by the setbacks of 1996.
"The government jumped but not far enough," Mayer said. "Things will have to get worse before they get better."
